{{Short description|Theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hadamard's lemma''', named after [[Jacques Hadamard]], is essentially a first-order form of [[Taylor's theorem]], in which we can express a smooth, real-valued function exactly in a convenient manner.

== Statement ==

{{math theorem|name=Hadamard's lemma{{sfn|Nestruev|2020|pp=17-18}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
Let <math>f</math> be a smooth, real-valued function defined on an open, [[star-convex]] [[Neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]] <math>U</math> of a point <math>a</math> in <math>n</math>-dimensional Euclidean space.  Then <math>f(x)</math> can be expressed, for all <math>x \in U,</math> in the form:
<math display="block">f(x) = f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i - a_i\right) g_i(x),</math>
where each <math>g_i</math> is a smooth function on <math>U,</math> <math>a = \left(a_1, \ldots, a_n\right),</math> and <math>x = \left(x_1, \ldots, x_n\right).</math>
}}

=== Proof ===

{{math proof|drop=hidden|proof= 
Let <math>x \in U.</math> Define <math>h : [0, 1] \to \R</math> by
<math display="block">h(t) = f(a + t(x - a)) \qquad \text{ for all } t \in [0, 1].</math>

Then 
<math display="block">h'(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a + t(x - a)) \left(x_i - a_i\right),</math>
which implies
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}h(1) - h(0)&= \int_0^1 h'(t)\,dt\\
&= \int_0^1 \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a + t(x - a)) \left(x_i - a_i\right)\, dt\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i - a_i\right)\int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a + t(x - a))\, dt.\end{aligned}</math>

But additionally, <math>h(1) - h(0) = f(x) - f(a),</math> so by letting
<math display="block">g_i(x) = \int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a + t(x - a))\, dt,</math>
the theorem has been proven. 
<math>\blacksquare</math>
}}

== Consequences and applications ==

{{math theorem|name=Corollary{{sfn|Nestruev|2020|pp=17-18}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
If <math>f : \R \to \R</math> is smooth and <math>f(0) = 0</math> then <math>f(x)/x</math> is a smooth function on <math>\R.</math> 
Explicitly, this conclusion means that the function <math>\R \to \R</math> that sends <math>x \in \R</math> to 
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
f(x)/x & \text{ if } x \neq 0 \\
\lim_{t \to 0} f(t)/t & \text{ if } x = 0 \\
\end{cases}</math>
is a well-defined smooth function on <math>\R.</math> 
}}

{{math proof|drop=hidden|proof= 
By Hadamard's lemma, there exists some <math>g \in C^{\infty}(\R)</math> such that <math>f(x) = f(0) + x g(x)</math> so that <math>f(0) = 0</math> implies <math>f(x)/x = g(x).</math> 
<math>\blacksquare</math>
}}

{{math theorem|name=Corollary{{sfn|Nestruev|2020|pp=17-18}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
If <math>y, z \in \R^n</math> are distinct points and <math>f : \R^n \to \R</math> is a smooth function that satisfies <math>f(z) = 0 = f(y)</math> then there exist smooth functions <math>g_i, h_i \in C^{\infty}\left(\R^n\right)</math> (<math>i = 1, \ldots, 3n - 2</math>) satisfying <math>g_i(z) = 0 = h_i(y)</math> for every <math>i</math> such that
<math display="block">f = \sum_{i}^{} g_i h_i.</math>
}}

{{math proof|drop=hidden|proof= 
By applying an [[Invertible function|invertible]] [[Affine map|affine linear]] change in coordinates, it may be assumed without loss of generality that <math>z = (0, \ldots, 0)</math> and <math>y = (0, \ldots, 0, 1).</math> 
By Hadamard's lemma, there exist <math>g_1, \ldots, g_n \in C^{\infty}\left(\R^n\right)</math> such that
<math>f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i g_i(x).</math>
For every <math>i = 1, \ldots, n,</math> let <math>\alpha_i := g_i(y)</math> where <math>0 = f(y) = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i g_i(y) = g_n(y)</math> implies <math>\alpha_n = 0.</math>
Then for any <math>x = \left(x_1, \ldots, x_n\right) \in \R^n,</math> 
<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{8}
f(x) 
&= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i g_i(x) && \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \left[x_i\left(g_i(x) - \alpha_i\right)\right] + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \left[x_i \alpha_i\right] && \quad \text{ using } g_i(x) = \left(g_i(x) - \alpha_i\right) + \alpha_i \text{ and } \alpha_n = 0 \\
&= \left[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\left(g_i(x) - \alpha_i\right)\right] + \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} x_i x_n \alpha_i\right] + \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} x_i \left(1 - x_n\right) \alpha_i\right] && \quad \text{ using } x_i = x_n x_i + x_i \left(1 - x_n\right). \\
\end{alignat}</math>
Each of the <math>3 n - 2</math> terms above has the desired properties. 
<math>\blacksquare</math>
}}
